Q: How to avoid repetitive usage of function in Oracle select query A:

Don't use a self-join. Use a CASE expression to only execute the function when regulation is reference_id to get the document_availability for those rows and set all the other rows to no and then wrap the query in an inline view and use an analytic function to update all the rows in the same partition based on the function's results.

SELECT item_no,
       item_type,
       regulation,
       document_type,
       MAX(document_availability) OVER (
         PARTITION BY item_no, item_type, regulation
       ) AS document_availability
FROM   (
  SELECT item_no,
         item_type,
         regulation,
         document_type,
         CASE
         WHEN document_type = 'reference_id'
         THEN f(item_no, item_type, regulation)
         ELSE 'no'
         END AS document_availability
  FROM   table_name
)

Which for the sample data and an example of a slow function that sleeps for 1 second each time it is run:

CREATE TABLE table_name (Item_no, item_type, regulation, document_type) AS
SELECT 10001, 'ACS', 'EU', 'reference_id' FROM DUAL UNION ALL
SELECT 10001, 'ACS', 'EU', 'prog_code'    FROM DUAL UNION ALL
SELECT 10001, 'ACS', 'US', 'reference_id' FROM DUAL UNION ALL
SELECT 10001, 'ACS', 'US', 'prog_code'    FROM DUAL UNION ALL
SELECT 10002, 'ATR', 'EU', 'reference_id' FROM DUAL UNION ALL
SELECT 10002, 'ATR', 'EU', 'dep_code'     FROM DUAL

CREATE FUNCTION f(
  i_item_no    TABLE_NAME.ITEM_NO%TYPE,
  i_item_type  TABLE_NAME.ITEM_TYPE%TYPE,
  i_regulation TABLE_NAME.REGULATION%TYPE
) RETURN VARCHAR2
IS
BEGIN
  DBMS_SESSION.SLEEP(1);
  RETURN CASE
         WHEN i_item_no = 10001
         AND  i_item_type = 'ACS'
         AND  i_regulation = 'EU'
         THEN 'yes'
         ELSE 'no'
         END;
END;
/

Then the output is:

ITEM_NO ITEM_TYPE REGULATION DOCUMENT_TYPE DOCUMENT_AVAILABILITY
10001 ACS EU reference_id yes
10001 ACS EU prog_code yes
10001 ACS US reference_id no
10001 ACS US prog_code no
10002 ATR EU reference_id no
10002 ATR EU dep_code no

And the function is only executed for the rows that have the required document_type (so it only takes 3 seconds to run with the slow function, and not 6 seconds).

The EXPLAIN PLAN for the query is simply:

Id Operation Name Rows Bytes Cost (%CPU) Time
0 SELECT STATEMENT 6 138 4 (25) 00:00:01
1 WINDOW SORT 6 138 4 (25) 00:00:01
2 TABLE ACCESS FULL TABLE_NAME 6 138 3 (0) 00:00:01

Q: Tkinter - Geometry management A:

Basic knowlege about tkinters geometry management

The geometry management of tkinter is characterized by this Quote here:

By default a top-level window appears on the screen in its natural size, which is the one determined internally by its widgets and geometry managers.

Toplevels

Your Toplevel is the first question you should have to answer with:

  • wm_geometry: size, position in your screen?
  • wm_minsize \ wm_maxsize are there minimal or maximal bounderies?
  • wm_resizable has the user the ability to resize it?
  • wm_attributes are there attributes like topmost or fullscreen?
  • pack_propagate \ grid_propagate ignore requested width and height of children.

Note: You can skip this question and let the process decide what will be needed after all.

Arrange children

To arrange your children you've got 3 options, each of them are designed to satisfy specific needs:

The packer:

The pack command is used to communicate with the packer, a geometry manager that arranges the children of a parent by packing them in order around the edges of the parent.

-> I use pack to arrange quickly a few widgets beside eachother in the master.

The placer

The placer is a geometry manager for Tk. It provides simple fixed placement of windows, where you specify the exact size and location of one window, called the slave, within another window, called the master. The placer also provides rubber-sheet placement, where you specify the size and location of the slave in terms of the dimensions of the master, so that the slave changes size and location in response to changes in the size of the master. Lastly, the placer allows you to mix these styles of placement so that, for example, the slave has a fixed width and height but is centered inside the master.

-> I use place sometimes for One-Sheet applications or to set a background image.

The gridder

The grid command is used to communicate with the grid geometry manager that arranges widgets in rows and columns inside of another window, called the geometry master (or master window).

-> Grid is the best choice for more complex applications that contains many widgets.

So the question you need to answer here, before picking one of these managers is, how do I organise my application in the best way?

Note:

Warning: Never mix grid and pack in the same master window. Tkinter will happily spend the rest of your lifetime trying to negotiate a solution that both managers are happy with. Instead of waiting, kill the application, and take another look at your code. A common mistake is to use the wrong parent for some of the widgets.

-> You can create a nested layout, in each master(window/frame) you've freedom of choice

Most important features

Most important features of each manger can help to answer your question. Because you will need to know if the manager can do what you wanna do.

For pack I think it is:

  1. fill stretch the slave horizontally, vertically or both
  2. expand The slaves should be expanded to consume extra space in their master.
  3. side Specifies which side of the master the slave(s) will be packed against.
  4. anchor it specifies where to position each slave in its parcel.

See this answer to understand the difference between fill and expand.

For place it should be:

  1. relheight -relheight=1.0, -height=-2 makes the slave 2 pixels shorter than the master.
  2. relwidth -relwidth=1.0, -width=5 makes the slave 5 pixels wider than the master.
  3. relx -relx=0.5, -x=-2 positions the left edge of the slave 2 pixels to the left out of the center.
  4. rely -rely=0.5, -x=3 positions the top edge of the slave 3 pixels below the center of its master.

And for grid it should be:

  1. columnspan Insert the slave so that it occupies n columns in the grid.
  2. rowspan Insert the slave so that it occupies n rows in the grid.
  3. sticky this option may be used to position (or stretch) the slave within its cell.
  4. grid_remove the configuration options for that window are remembered
  5. grid_columnconfigure
  6. grid_rowconfigure

for the last two options I recommend this answer here.

Read the docs

A working exampel to play with can be found here:

#you will notice if you swip right with center.

Q: Why does the Tkinter canvas-leave event behave differently in Windows 11 and Linux Mint? A:

I'm under windows 11 and have the exact same behavior as you stated under linux mint. Which is logical

-> `<Enter-Frame>`-> `<Leave-Frame>` -> `<Leave-Canvas>`-> `<Leave-Window>`
-> `<Enter-Window>` -> `<Enter-Canvas>`

That been said, it's entirely up to the window manager of the OS to post such Events, tkinter does not generate them, tkinter respond to the events.

How can I avoid such problems?

It's not clear what you try to accomplish. Generally speaking, it's a sign of bad code if you over and over bind and unbind events. Extract the important information of the event and handle it the way you want.

Q: Difference between "fill" and "expand" options for tkinter pack method A:

The pack geometry algorithm allocates a "frame" (a rectangle) and is called a parcel.
The parcel for top or bottom is the initial free width of the container and the height of the widget you want to pack in the container.

The -fill option lets you expand the widget, while the -expand option lets you expand the the parcel.

So for a top or bottom packed widget you can see (nearly) always a effect for by filling the x direction.
If you want to fill in y or both direction as well, you have to extend the parcel first.

Contrary for left or right packed widgets, where the parcel is the initial free height of the container and the width of the widget you want to pack.

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()

label = tk.Label(text='This widget is at the top',bg='red')
label2 = tk.Label(text='This widget is at the bottom',bg='green')
label3 = tk.Label(text='Left\nHand\nSide',bg='yellow')
label4 = tk.Label(text='Right\nHand\nSide',bg='blue')
label5 = tk.Label(text="This layout is like Java's BorderLayout",bg='white')

label.pack(side='top',fill='x')
label2.pack(side='bottom',fill='x')
label3.pack(side='left',fill='y')
label4.pack(side='right', fill='y')
label5.pack(fill='both',expand=True) #note that no side parameter means "center"

root.mainloop()

That's why the order of packing the widgets is important by building semi-complex layouts with the pack manager.
If you were to pack left or right before the bottom one, you would have consumed the space where the bottom widget is supposed to be.
